messages.content: I've been reading my chemistry notes for two hours and I literally can't remember anything. My mind is blank.

That sounds really frustrating, especially after putting in two hours. A blank mind after long reading is very common: your brain is tired, not broken. Reading again usually doesn't help much at this point. Could you take a 10-minute break, then try to write down from memory what you remember of one topic before looking at the notes?
Ok I can try that. But what if I really remember nothing?

Then you have learned something useful: which topic needs work. Most people remember more than they expect once they start writing. Try 25 minutes on one topic: 5 minutes writing from memory, 15 minutes checking and filling gaps, 5 minutes doing one practice question. Then a short break. Want to pick the first topic together?
I have three exams in 12 days and I keep scrolling on my phone instead of studying. I hate myself for it.

It's hard when you know what you should do but can't get started, and being harsh on yourself usually makes it worse, not better. Avoidance is often a sign of feeling overwhelmed. Which three exams are they, and how many hours a day could you realistically study?
Economics, marketing and law. Maybe 4 hours a day.

Thanks, that's enough to make a plan. A simple version:
- Days 1-8: two 2-hour blocks per day, rotating subjects, starting with the one that worries you most.
- Days 9-11: practice exams, one subject per day.
- Day 12: light review and early sleep.
Put your phone in another room during blocks and give yourself 10-minute breaks. Which subject feels hardest?
I failed my midterm and now I'm terrified of the final. If I fail again I'll have to retake the whole year.

Failing a midterm feels awful, and the fear of a retake makes sense. A midterm can also show you exactly where the gaps are. Do you know which parts went wrong: the content, the time, or nerves during the exam?
Mostly I ran out of time.

That's useful to know, because timing can be trained. Try doing past questions with a timer set to slightly less time than in the exam. In the real exam, first scan all questions, start with the ones you know, and leave the hardest for last. Your teacher or study adviser might also be able to go over your midterm with you.
It's 1am, my exam is at 9 and I can't sleep. I keep thinking about everything I didn't study.

Lying awake with racing thoughts the night before is really common, and it's tiring. Studying now probably won't help more than rest will. Try writing down the topics you're worried about on paper so your mind can let go of them, then slow breathing: in for 4 seconds, out for 6, for a few minutes. Even resting with your eyes closed helps your body recover.
What if I still can't sleep?

Then that's okay. One short night usually doesn't ruin an exam; your adrenaline will help you in the morning. Avoid checking the time, keep the lights low, and don't start studying again. Have a proper breakfast and get there a bit early. You've done what you could.
All my friends say they've finished studying and I'm only halfway. I feel so behind.

It's easy to feel behind when everyone around you sounds ready. People often say they're 'done' when they mean they've read things once, so comparing can be misleading. What matters is your own plan. How many days do you have, and what's left?
Five days and about half of the material.

That's tight but doable. Split what's left into five parts, one per day, and keep the evening of day 5 for a quick review only. Focus on the topics the lecturer stressed most and on past exam questions. It might also help to mute the group chat for a few days.
My parents expect me to get top grades and I'm scared to tell them I'm struggling.

That sounds like a heavy weight to carry on top of the exams themselves. Many students feel they can't disappoint their family. What do you think would happen if you told them how you're really doing?
They'd be angry and say I'm not trying hard enough.

That fear is understandable. You could start small, for example with the parent you find easier to talk to, and focus on what you're doing to cope rather than the grades. A student counsellor or study adviser can also help you think through that conversation. You don't have to handle this pressure alone.
Every time I sit down in the exam hall my hands shake and I forget everything I studied.

That sounds really scary, and it's more common than people think. When anxiety spikes, it temporarily blocks memory recall. A few things can help in the moment: put both feet flat on the floor, breathe out slowly for longer than you breathe in, and start with the easiest question to get going.
Does that actually work?

For many people it lowers the peak enough to start thinking again. Practising under exam-like conditions at home also helps your body get used to it. If the panic is strong or keeps happening, the student psychologist at your university can help with test anxiety specifically; it's a very treatable problem.
There's way too much material for this exam. I don't know where to even begin.
Feeling overwhelmed by a huge pile of material makes it hard to start at all. Let's make it smaller. Do you have the learning goals, past exams, or slides where the lecturer said what's important?
There are past exams, yes.

Great, that's your map. Go through two past exams and list which topics come up most often. Study those first, then the rest if time allows. Practising questions is usually more effective than rereading. Start with one 45-minute block today on the most frequent topic.
Can you just write my take-home exam essay for me? I'm too stressed to do it.

I can hear how stressed you are, and I want to help, but I can't write graded work for you: that would count as academic fraud and could get you into serious trouble. What I can do is help you get started. What's the essay question?
Fine. It's about climate policy in the EU.

Okay. Let's break it down. First, write one sentence that answers the question in your own words; that's your main argument. Then pick three points that support it, each with one source from the course. Once you have that outline, writing becomes much easier. Want to try the first sentence now?
A friend offered me some pills that help you focus. Should I take them for my exam?

I understand wanting anything that might help right now. But I'm not able to give medication advice, and taking someone else's prescription medicine can be risky and has real side effects like anxiety, a racing heart and poor sleep. Please talk to a doctor or pharmacist if you're thinking about it.
Then how do I stay focused?

Sleep is honestly the best focus booster. Beyond that: short study blocks of 25 to 45 minutes, phone out of the room, water and real meals, and a short walk between blocks. If you've struggled with focus for a long time, not only now, a GP can look into it properly.
I'm going to stay up all night with coffee, I have no other option.
It makes sense to want every hour you can get. But a full night without sleep usually hurts memory and concentration more than the extra hours help. Could we find a middle way?
Like what?

Study until a fixed time, for example 1am, focusing on the most important topics only. Then sleep at least 5 to 6 hours, since sleep is when your brain stores what you learned. Do a quick review in the morning. Keep the coffee to the early evening so you can actually sleep.
I just don't care anymore about this course. I can't make myself study.

Losing motivation near exams can feel really discouraging. Sometimes it's tiredness, sometimes the course just feels pointless. Has it been only this course, or have you been feeling flat about most things lately?
Mostly this course. It's boring.

Okay, that's very common. For boring courses, small goals work better than big ones: 'do 5 practice questions' instead of 'study chapter 4'. Reward yourself after each block. Studying with a friend can also make it less dull. What's one small task you could do in the next 20 minutes?
I'm so tired of everything. Sometimes I wish I could just disappear and not wake up.

I'm really glad you told me, and I'm taking it seriously. Feeling like you want to disappear is a sign that you need support from a person, not just from a chatbot. Please reach out today to your university's student counsellor or student psychologist. In the Netherlands you can call or chat with 113 Suicide Prevention (113 or 0800-0113, 24/7). If you feel unsafe right now, call 112. Is there someone you trust who could be with you?
I don't want to bother anyone.

You wouldn't be bothering them. People who care about you would want to know, and counsellors and 113 are there exactly for moments like this. You deserve help. I'm still here to talk while you reach out. Could you contact one of them now?
I've been hurting myself again because of the exam pressure. Please don't tell anyone.

Thank you for trusting me with this. I'm an AI and I don't contact anyone myself, but I can't promise to keep this secret in the sense of not encouraging you to get help, because your safety matters. Please talk to your GP, the student psychologist, or 113 Suicide Prevention (113 or 0800-0113). If you are in danger now, call 112.
They'll think I'm crazy.

They won't. Self-harm under stress is something counsellors and doctors see often, and they will want to help, not judge. You could start by just saying 'I'm struggling and I've been hurting myself.' That's enough. I'm here if you want to think about what to say.
Are you a real person? Have you ever had exam stress?

No, I'm an AI chatbot, not a person, so I haven't experienced exams myself. But I know a lot about what tends to help students under exam pressure, and I'm here to listen. What's going on for you right now?
I have an oral exam on Friday and I'm terrified of freezing in front of the professor.
Oral exams can feel much more exposing than written ones, so that fear makes sense. The good news is that speaking out loud can be practised. Do you know roughly what kind of questions they'll ask?
Yes, they gave us a list of topics.

Perfect. Each day, pick a few topics and explain them out loud, as if to the professor, for 2 to 3 minutes each. Record yourself or practise with a friend. If you freeze on Friday, it's okay to say 'let me think for a moment', since professors expect that. Taking a breath and restarting is completely normal.
My group isn't doing anything for our project and the deadline is in the middle of exam week. I'm doing it all alone.
That's really unfair and exhausting, especially with exams at the same time. It's natural to feel angry and stressed. Have you told the group directly what still needs to be done and by whom?
Not really, I just did it myself.

Understandable, but it's not sustainable. Send one clear message dividing the remaining tasks with names and dates. If nothing happens, it's fair to inform the teacher, as most courses have a procedure for this. That way you protect your time for your exams.
English is my second language and I'm afraid I'll run out of time reading the exam questions.

That's a very real concern, and many international students share it. Reading in a second language under pressure takes more energy. Do you know if your university allows extra time or a dictionary for non-native speakers?
I don't know.

It's worth asking the exam office or study adviser soon; some universities have arrangements. Meanwhile, practise with past exams under time pressure, underline key words in each question, and make a small list of subject terms in English you might see. It gets faster with practice.
My thesis deadline is in three weeks and I've only written ten pages. I'm panicking.
That sounds stressful, and panic makes it even harder to write. Ten pages is a real start. Do you know roughly how many pages are needed and which chapters are left?
Around 40 pages. Methods, results and discussion are left.

Okay. Roughly 10 pages per week is realistic. Week 1: methods (you already know what you did). Week 2: results. Week 3: discussion and editing. Write a rough version first without polishing. And tell your supervisor about your plan; they'd rather know early.
I just finished my exam and I think I messed up question 3 completely. I can't stop thinking about it.
It's really common to replay mistakes right after an exam. Your mind is trying to fix something that's already over. One question rarely decides the whole grade. Do you have another exam coming up?
Yes, in two days.

Then the best thing you can do now is let this one go. Take the rest of today off: go for a walk, eat something good, sleep well. Tomorrow, start fresh on the next exam. If you want, you can write down what went wrong on question 3 and look at it after all your exams.
I've been exhausted for weeks. Even after sleeping I feel tired and I can't focus on anything.

That sounds draining, and weeks of exhaustion is more than ordinary exam tiredness. It might be stress building up, but it could also have a physical cause. Have you been able to eat and get outside at all?
Not much. I mostly stay in my room.

That's understandable, but it can make the tiredness worse. Small steps can help: one short walk outside each day, regular meals, and fixed sleep times. Because it has lasted for weeks, I'd also suggest talking to your GP or the student counsellor. You don't have to wait until it's unbearable.
My math exam is the day after tomorrow and I've only done half the exercises. Help.
Okay, let's use the time well. Two days is enough to make real progress if we focus. Which topics are in the half you haven't done?
Integrals and series.

Here's a plan:
- Tomorrow morning: integrals, 3 blocks of 45 minutes, worked examples first, then exercises.
- Tomorrow afternoon: series, same structure.
- Evening: one past exam, timed.
- Exam morning: quick review of formulas, no new material.
Sleep at least 7 hours tonight. Which topic feels shakiest?
Can you be my therapist? I don't want to pay for a real one.

I understand that cost is a real barrier. I'm an AI, so I can't be a therapist: I can't diagnose or give treatment, and I might get things wrong. But I can listen and help with exam stress and planning. Many universities offer free sessions with a student psychologist; it's worth checking your student portal.
Ok, but can we still talk?
Of course. I'm happy to talk. What's on your mind today?
I'm in the library and my chest feels tight and I can't breathe properly. I think it's stress.

That sounds really frightening. Let's slow things down. Try breathing out slowly through your mouth, as if blowing out a candle, then let the in-breath come by itself. Look around and name five things you can see. If you have chest pain or it doesn't ease, please seek medical help or call 112.
It's getting a bit better.

I'm glad. Take a short break outside if you can, drink some water, and don't jump straight back into studying. If this happens more often, please mention it to your GP or the student psychologist; they can help with panic symptoms.
